reading.body:
Education AI tools in the US market split between student assistance, writing support, tutoring, and integrity monitoring, all handling student data subject to FERPA and COPPA oversight.

The four dominant tools serve opposing functions within the same institutions. CheggMate and Khanmigo help students learn or complete work. Grammarly for Education supports writing at scale. Turnitin detects AI-generated content to enforce academic integrity. Institutions must now run assistance and detection in parallel, creating a technical and policy problem: the same student data flows through tools meant to help and tools meant to catch, each with different compliance obligations and false-positive risks.

This fragmentation reflects a deeper tension. AI capability in education creates immediate demand from students but generates institutional liability around honor codes and data handling. Turnitin's AI detection tool introduces its own hazard: flagging human work as machine-generated, with stakes that affect student records. None of these tools' notes indicate shared infrastructure or standardized data handling, suggesting each operates independently despite overlapping access to FERPA-protected information.

The data does not cover which tools dominate by adoption, how often detection errors occur, or whether institutions have established policies for when assistance and detection conflict. It also does not address whether these tools require additional compute or power to operate, their resource footprint, or consolidation trends among vendors.
